supportingExcerpt: Lineage describes descent from earlier cells. A cell type or identity describes a differentiated family, while a state describes context-dependent features such as activation, stress or cycling. A genetic clone has shared ancestry and can be tracked through specified genomic features; an RNA cluster alone does not establish that ancestry. Stem cells can renew and generate descendants; progenitor potential is restricted by the biological context. Differentiation develops specialized properties without requiring every change of state to become a new lineage.
Pattern or module score, subtype classifier and outcome predictor answer different questions; performance belongs to a population, endpoint and horizon.

Epithelium forms linings, coverings and glands; an epithelial cell is not necessarily malignant. A basement membrane is extracellular supporting material beneath an epithelium, distinct from each cell’s lipid membrane. Stroma includes supporting cells, extracellular matrix and vascular structures, rather than only collagen or fibroblasts. Immune cells and other nonmalignant cells can contribute to a tumor specimen. The relevant compartments depend on the tissue and disease.

Support a malignant-cell assignment with tissue context, a coherent marker panel, suitable normal references and quality checks, rather than one marker or cluster name. In five primary glioblastomas, Patel and colleagues profiled 430 cells and inferred broad chromosome alterations by averaging RNA expression along chromosomes against normal reference profiles. This was RNA-based inference, not a direct DNA copy count or a breast diagnostic rule. A flat inferred profile can miss a malignant cell lacking a detectable broad change; focal alterations and point mutations can also be missed. Matched DNA, pathology and spatial evidence can corroborate an assignment, but bulk DNA does not identify every RNA barcode. Mixed markers may reflect ambient RNA or doublets. In another fictional mixed sample, vimentin RNA could come from fibroblasts or a changed cancer-cell programme. Even cell-attributed expression of that marker alone does not establish invasion, resistance or ancestry. Keep uncertain assignments uncertain.

In a fictional set with separately established shared genetic ancestry, one cell is cycling and another is noncycling. Different activity labels do not require different ancestry. Conversely, two cells in the same RNA cluster need not belong to the same genetic clone. The origin of the ancestry label matters: expression resemblance alone does not establish it.
Controlled perturbations deliberately change specified factors and compare responses with suitable controls. A model response alone does not prove its mechanism or patient benefit.
Analytical repeatability, clinical validity and clinical utility are separate questions.

There is no universal IHC scoring scale or positivity threshold. Retain antibody clone, retrieval and detection method, controls, eligible cells, subcellular location, intensity, distribution and intended use. A research stain does not automatically replace a clinical selection assay.
Total copy number counts copies of a region; allele-specific copy number estimates the contributions of the distinguishable sequence versions A and B.
1+1 is two copies with both versions; 1+0 is one copy with LOH (deletion); 2+0 is copy-neutral LOH (two copies, one version); 2+1 is three copies with both versions retained.

Methods combine relative coverage with allele balance at informative heterozygous sites, segment the genome and fit states; a matched normal helps; a total-copy profile alone cannot separate 1+1 from 2+0; homozygous sites are uninformative.

At a diploid location, heterozygous means that the two copies differ in the feature being considered; homozygous means they match. Hemizygous describes a single copy in the specified context. Tumor gains, losses and genome doubling can make a two-copy model inadequate. Loss of heterozygosity means loss of previously different allelic information; it can accompany a deletion or occur while total copy count remains unchanged. Total copy number alone cannot identify which allele was retained.

A local LOH state and a genome-wide LOH score have different scope. In an idealised informative A/B region, 1+1 and 2+0 both total two copies, but only 2+0 loses one sequence version. A total-copy profile alone cannot distinguish them. Allele-aware inputs and purity/ploidy assumptions constrain the call; a genome-wide score does not identify the retained sequence, phase a mutation or directly measure current gene function.
Copy state does not establish phase, gene inactivity, expression, dependency or drug response; bulk fits can hide subpopulations and unsampled lesions.

Major and minor counts are the larger and smaller allelic contributions; minor of zero supports LOH under the model; they do not identify parental origin or assign a mutation to a copy; phasing needs suitable evidence.
Local copy count differs from ploidy; relative signal can fit different purity and ploidy pairs; fractional counts can reflect mixture or subclonal states.

Typical normal breast ducts and acini have luminal epithelial cells facing the lumen, an outer living myoepithelial layer, extracellular basement membrane and then stroma. Myoepithelial cells have contractile features that help move milk; they are not the chest muscle. Basement membrane contains matrix proteins such as laminins and type IV collagen, not living cells.

In a fictional comparison, gene R is high in cancer cells, low in fibroblasts and similarly high in normal luminal epithelial cells. The first contrast supports higher expression than fibroblasts, even if it passes a statistical threshold; it does not establish cancer selectivity. The normal epithelial comparison addresses that claim more closely, while leaving other organs, cell states and target accessibility untested. If that reference group is tiny, contaminated or prepared differently, preserve the unresolved comparison rather than declaring selectivity or exact equality. Normal epithelial cells can also contribute familiar lineage markers to a tumour specimen. An image-based tumour mask is an assignment that needs validation for its actual method and specimens, rather than automatic proof that every included cell is malignant.

RNA carries cellular messages; bulk sequencing samples those messages from combined tissue after protocol-specific capture and preparation. Analysis assigns usable observations to genes or transcripts and applies a defined comparison scale. A change can reflect cell composition, expression within cells or both. Gene totals can conceal transcript differences, and pooled RNA does not directly establish protein localisation, pathway flux or drug dependence.

Bulk RNA sequencing measures captured messages pooled across a specimen. Cancer, immune and supporting cells can contribute different amounts of RNA; a higher signal can reflect a changed mixture, changed expression within cells, or both. Zero detected reads does not establish biological absence. Source: Conesa et al., 2016 methods review, https://doi.org/10.1186/s13059-016-0881-8.

A tumour specimen can contain malignant, immune, stromal and normal cells. A difference in an aggregate molecular signal can reflect a changed mixture, changed expression within cells or both. That is different from a directly counted cell fraction or a density per sampled area, each of which also needs its denominator and sampled region.

Preparation can change what is recovered. Slyper and colleagues compared single-cell and single-nucleus profiling in matched tumour specimens and found similar cell types at sometimes different proportions. A recovered profile mixture is therefore not automatically the original tissue census. Deconvolution and purity models can help investigate contributions under assumptions; they do not certify the cell of origin of every signal or remove sampling differences.

Bulk RNA or protein measurements combine contributions from sampled cells. A stronger signal can reflect more cells of one type, changed expression within cells, or both. Spatial review and suitable cell markers help test attribution; a mixed-tissue result should not automatically be assigned to cancer cells. Normal and cancer breast atlases provide defined examples of this cellular diversity.

TIL is a location label, CD8 is a phenotype and antigen specificity is another property. Simoni found bystander CD8 cells recognizing viral rather than cancer epitopes in human lung and colorectal tumours; the study’s CD39 associations are not a universal test of every cell’s target. A functional assay compares defined effectors and targets with recognition and target-survival controls. Neither presence, cytokine release nor one killing assay reproduces every access barrier or establishes clinical benefit.
Binding predictors estimate whether a peptide can fit a specified allele's groove, but processing, transport, loading and surface expression decide whether it is displayed.

An antibody may recognize an epitope on more than one product form or a remaining fragment. Many mass-spectrometry workflows digest proteins into peptides: a shared detected peptide cannot distinguish every full-length form. A candidate peptide sequence also does not establish its display by HLA. Separate assays address amount, location, intact form, function and antigen presentation.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

Sequencing reports sampled receptor identities and abundances under an operational clonotype definition. Paired alpha-beta identities are more complete than beta alone. Peptide-HLA multimer binding, stimulus-induced cellular response, target-cell death and clinical benefit are different endpoints. Include irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls; peptide-loaded cells can bypass natural processing.

These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display.

A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Consider an invented repair-gene R example, with measurements attributed to the same pretreatment tissue region except for a derived model. A supported splice-site DNA variant identifies a candidate sequence change. Loss of the other allelic contribution, with the variant assigned to the retained contribution, supports a possible two-hit explanation subject to copy and phase uncertainty. A reproducible abnormal RNA junction in malignant-cell-enriched material adds evidence for a changed transcript product, while reduced staining with suitable controls adds a protein-signal difference in the assigned cells. Neither establishes that every intact protein is gone. A high genomic scar adds evidence about genomic history, not a direct test of present repair. Impaired repair in a suitable model with informative cycling and damage controls addresses function under those conditions. A replicated drug response at specified exposures adds a model-sensitivity hypothesis; it still leaves achievable safe exposure and patient benefit to their appropriate evidence. These are distinct observations, not a requirement to perform every assay before using any established clinical biomarker.

Zheng and colleagues' 2017 droplet study grouped PCR duplicates by a shared partition barcode, UMI and gene assignment after its quality filters. In a fictional example, three qualifying reads in one such group count as one captured molecule; the same tag in another gene or partition is not automatically the same molecule. A UMI is a random sequence tag, rather than a globally unique name. Smith and colleagues showed that tag errors distort molecule estimates and described limits as the available tag diversity is used up. Retain the chemistry, grouping and error handling: the count is not a census of RNA originally present, proof of one cell per barcode or a protein measurement.
A barcode labels a reaction compartment and a UMI separates captured molecules from amplified copies, giving a gene-by-barcode table; a barcode does not guarantee one intact cell.

RNA is distributed across cellular compartments. Whole-cell and nucleus preparations sample different material and can recover different populations. Barcodes label captured profiles rather than certifying one intact cell; quality, ambient RNA and doublet checks remain necessary. Sparse capture and selective recovery prevent a complete census, and many profiles from one biopsy do not create independent patient replicates.

A detection fraction uses the analysed profiles and a stated detection rule: it is not automatically the fraction of all cells in the original tissue. A profile with one immune-gene count but otherwise epithelial features is not thereby identified as an immune cell. Sparse recovery, ambient RNA and more than one contributing cell can complicate its interpretation. Check coherent marker evidence and the method of assignment; a mixture of markers does not by itself establish a new cell type. Pooling the counts from a selected set of profiles is pseudobulk. Five hundred nuclei from one biopsy can summarize that selected population, while the biopsy remains one biological specimen rather than five hundred independent patients.

Background correction estimates which part of a profile comes from free RNA in the preparation. SoupX's authors discuss deliberately overcorrecting contamination at the cost of removing a small amount of genuine signal. The estimated contamination and settings therefore need review; a corrected weak count or zero is not an infallible label of the molecule's origin.
A zero can be a missed molecule (dropout) rather than absence; ambient RNA contaminates profiles; a doublet combines cells or nuclei; correction does not certify every barcode.

RNA abundance reflects production, processing and degradation. Short sequencing reads do not prove that a full-length intact message was captured. A noncoding RNA can function without becoming a protein, and reverse transcription copies RNA into DNA in relevant biological contexts. RNA amount does not determine a fixed protein amount or activity.

Amino acids join through peptide bonds into polypeptide chains; linked amino acids are residues. Peptide and protein usage overlaps without a universal length boundary. A protein may contain one or several chains, folded domains and flexible regions. Processing, chemical modifications, localization, production and degradation affect its form and behavior. Genes specify coding templates, but a DNA or RNA finding does not measure the resulting protein’s intact structure or activity.

A barcode identifies a captured reaction profile, requiring checks for ambient RNA and multiple contributing cells. Whole-cell and isolated-nucleus preparations sample different compartments; recovered profiles are not a complete tissue census. A zero count does not establish biological absence. Sources: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28091601/ and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33367645/.

Staining recognises an antibody-defined molecular feature, or epitope, rather than automatically proving a complete functioning protein. In an invented repair-gene example, weaker staining in identified cancer cells than in normal neighbours supports a cell-specific signal difference if the controls are adequate. The antibody may recognise a fragment or more than one protein form, so this does not give the amount of intact useful repair protein. The relevant form and current repair need suitable measurements of their own. One validated method can sometimes answer several questions, but measuring one property does not establish every other one.

In a fictional experiment, receptor R is high in malignant cells, low in fibroblasts and similarly high in normal epithelial cells. A stain places it on cancer-cell membranes, while blocking R has little effect on growth under the tested conditions. This supports neither cancer selectivity nor a demonstrated growth dependency. R could be investigated as an antibody-drug-conjugate delivery address, but that hypothesis still needs evidence for binding, access, uptake where required, payload effect and relevant normal-tissue exposure. A plausible delivery address is not a promised drug response; enrichment, selectivity, engagement, dependence and clinical benefit are different claims.

Bulk receptor abundance and staining mainly on blood vessels can both be correct: one measures a mixture and the other locates signal. Neither establishes target accessibility or treatment benefit. Staining also does not establish protein activity or cancer-cell dependence on that protein.

A controlled perturbation deliberately changes a defined factor and measures the response against appropriate comparison conditions. Vehicle, positive, negative and mechanism controls answer different questions. A reproducible response can support an experimental claim without establishing its proposed mechanism or patient benefit. Baseline growth, timing, dose and the actual unit assigned to treatment matter.

A vehicle control contains the carrier without the active treatment; an untreated condition asks a different question if the carrier has effects. A positive control checks that the assay can detect a known relevant response, while a negative or non-targeting control estimates background under its design. Another independent way to disrupt the same function can support a mechanism, and a rescue restores a function to test whether that reverses the response here. Off-target effects, incomplete restoration and model context limit interpretation. These are questions for matched model, timing and readout; no one control proves specificity or patient benefit, and agreement between similar readouts is not automatically independent mechanistic confirmation.

Splicing processes an initial RNA transcript. Exons are retained in a specified product and may contain untranslated sequence; introns are removed. For many nuclear pre-mRNAs, a spliceosome made of RNA and proteins recognizes boundary and regulatory sequences. The donor site starts an intron and the acceptor site ends it. Alternative choices yield transcript isoforms; a variant can alter exon inclusion, intron retention or use of a cryptic site. Exon skipping is not automatically a frameshift: the coding sequence and resulting joins matter. An altered message may undergo nonsense-mediated decay or produce a changed protein, but neither outcome follows from a prediction alone.

Imagine separate precursor RNAs from the same fictional gene, with exons A, B and C in that order. One processing outcome retains A-B-C; another joins A directly to C. B is a skipped exon in the second outcome, rather than a region reclassified as an intron. One RNA molecule is not split into both complete products. These are selected outcomes across separate molecules, with other processing possibilities left open. Retained exon sequence can include untranslated regions. The letter pattern alone supplies neither a reading frame nor a guarantee about protein production or RNA decay.

A junction read supports a local RNA join, not necessarily a complete isoform. Gene-level counts can hide transcript differences. RNA quality, read coverage, reference version and cell mixture affect interpretation; protein quantity and function need separate evidence.

In the recipe analogy, the DNA template is retained while an RNA copy is assembled. Translation uses a message as instructions for joining amino acids; the RNA molecule is not the material converted into the protein. The arrows name these processes rather than showing that a reported DNA change produced a measured message or working product. Noncoding RNA lies outside this simplified protein-coding route. Questions about production, location and activity remain open until suitable evidence addresses them.

Replication makes DNA from DNA. Transcription uses a DNA template to make RNA. Translation reads the coding sequence of a message in three-base codons to build a polypeptide; the transcript and reading frame matter. Functional noncoding RNAs do not need to become protein. Reverse transcription copies RNA into DNA in relevant viral and retrotransposon contexts. This information-flow map is not a guarantee that every DNA change produces a measured RNA or protein change.

A protein-coding gene supplies RNA that can be translated into a polypeptide, while a noncoding RNA gene produces a functional RNA. Promoters and other regulatory regions influence transcription in a cell-dependent context. One gene can have several transcript versions. Exons are retained regions of a specified processed transcript and can include untranslated sequence; introns are removed by splicing. Coding sequence is the translated part of a coding message. A gene name alone does not specify a transcript, coding interval or protein product.
A drug target is the molecule or structure a treatment acts on and its mechanism of action is how that action produces an effect, and each step from target to patient benefit needs its own evidence.

CAP's morphology-based histological classification and supporting-marker assessment answer a tissue question. A schematic rim is neither an immunostain result nor a diagnosis; illustrated gaps or colours cannot establish invasion. Interpret the actual tissue architecture and appropriately controlled stains together.
